facts: Tyler dies, unnoticed.
Mr Acheson, Mrs Davenant's champion, calls Tyler 'Reverend'.
The narrator suggests Tyler may have learned Hebrew while reading for the Church.
Tyler never told the narrator anything about his own affairs.
The narrator judges that Tyler's black pessimism would have got him thrown out of any established Western church.
The scene is set on a midsummer night on the terrace of the Palace at Whitehall, overlooking the Thames.
The Palace clock chimes the quarters and strikes eleven.
A Beefeater is on guard when a cloaked man approaches.
The Beefeater challenges him to stand and give the password.
The Man says he has clean forgotten the word.
The Beefeater tells him he cannot pass and demands his business and identity.
The Beefeater tells the Man he speaks strangely but is a very civil gentleman.
The Beefeater says a poor man feels drawn to him because he shares his thoughts.
The Man replies that sharing thoughts is his trade, but the world mostly wants none of them.
The palace door opens from within and lamplight streams out.
The Beefeater announces that the Man's lady is coming and withdraws to the other end of his ward.
The Lady, sleepwalking, says what's done cannot be undone and cries 'Out' and 'Fie! a queen, and freckled!'
The Man shakes her arm and calls her Mary, asking if she is asleep.
The Lady wakes, starts, and nearly faints, and he catches her on his arm.
The Lady asks where she is and what he is.
The Man begs her pardon and says he mistook her for his mistress Mary.
The Lady is outraged and demands how he dares.
The Man says there is a power that can redeem them.
The Lady thanks him sarcastically for his sermon and says she knows her duty.
The Man insists it is not a sermon but the living truth.
The Man declares the power he means is the power of immortal poesy.
The Man says clothing vileness in a magical garment of words transfigures people and uplifts their souls.
The Man tells the Lady she is the head of his Church when she speaks as she did at first.
He quotes 'All the perfumes of Arabia' and doubts the Queen could speak thus.
He says the Queen is reputed to play well on the virginals, and if she played so to him he would kiss her hands.
He tells the Lady that until then she is his Queen and he will kiss her lips.
He puts his arms about her.
The Lady calls it unmeasured impudence and orders him to take his hands off her on his life.
Shakespear scrambles indignantly to his feet, protesting at being called base-born.
Shakespear declares he is a Shakespear of Stratford whose mother was an Arden.
Elizabeth, furious, swears and starts to threaten to teach him.
The Dark Lady rises from her knees and throws herself between them.
The Dark Lady begs Will not to anger the Queen further, saying it is death, and asks the Queen not to listen to him.
Shakespear refuses to flatter a monarch who forgets what is due to his family, even to save Mary's life or his own.
Shakespear says John Shakespear married only once while Harry Tudor married six times.
Shakespear tells Elizabeth she should blush to utter her father's name.
The Dark Lady cries out to Will for pity's sake while Elizabeth calls him an insolent dog.
Shakespear cuts them short by asking Elizabeth how she knows King Harry was really her father.
Elizabeth swears and stops to grind her teeth with rage.
The Dark Lady laments that she will be whipped through the streets.
Shakespear tells Elizabeth to learn to know herself better.
The Dark Lady begins to swear to the Queen as she hopes for salvation.
Shakespear interjects a sardonic 'Ha!'
The Dark Lady angrily retorts that she is as likely to be saved as he who believes in nothing but black magic of words and verses.
The Dark Lady tells the Queen she came there to break with Shakespear for ever.
The Dark Lady says Shakespear anatomizes a woman's soul and wrings tears of blood from her humiliation.
The Dark Lady says he then heals the wound with flatteries no woman can resist.
The Dark Lady warns the Queen that Shakespear is flattering her even as he speaks.
Elizabeth's eye flashes terribly and she says 'Is it so?'
Shakespear tells the Queen the Dark Lady is jealous, and not without reason.
Shakespear reproaches the Queen for cruelly hiding her royal dignity when she found him there.
Shakespear says he can never be content with the black-haired devil again after looking on real beauty and real majesty.
Shakespear says he would have the Queen think him great enough to grant him a boon.
Elizabeth hopes it is a boon that may be asked of a virgin Queen without offence.
Elizabeth says she mistrusts his forwardness and bids him remember she does not let persons of his degree presume too far.
Elizabeth refers mockingly to his father the alderman.
Shakespear promises not to forget himself again.
Shakespear says that if he could make her a serving wench she would remain neither queen nor virgin for long.
Shakespear says he is not there to write the Queen's plays for her.
Shakespear tells Elizabeth she is there to inspire them and was ordained for it.
Shakespear asks her to endow a great playhouse, coining the name 'National Theatre' for it.
Elizabeth objects that there are already theatres enough on the Bankside and in Blackfriars.
Shakespear argues that endowment would encourage other men to take up playwriting who now despise it.
Shakespear says play-writing is left to those whose counsels do little good to the realm.
Shakespear claims plays form the minds and affections of men.
Shakespear says whatever men see done on the stage they will soon do in earnest in the world, which is a larger stage.
Shakespear urges the Queen to take up the work the Church has abandoned and restore playing to its former dignity.
Elizabeth says she will speak of the matter to the Lord Treasurer.
Shakespear says he is then undone, since no Lord Treasurer ever found a penny except for a war or a salary for his own nephew.
Elizabeth admits Shakespear speaks the truth but says she cannot mend it.
Elizabeth calls out to ask who keeps ward on the queen's lodgings that night.
The Warder answers that he does.
Elizabeth orders him to keep watch better in future, saying he let a dangerous gallant reach her chamber door.
Elizabeth orders the Warder to lead Shakespear out and bring her word when he is locked out.
Elizabeth says she will scarcely dare undress until the palace gates are between them.
Shakespear kisses her hand and says his body goes out into the darkness but his thoughts follow her.
Clodagh is five years older than the narrator and five years older than her nephew.
Clodagh's nephew was born from her sister's marriage to Peters of Taunton.
The nephew is Peter Peters, who is to join the Boreal expedition as doctor, botanist and meteorological assistant.
On the day of Clark's visit, the narrator tells Clodagh within five minutes that Dr Clark has been talking to him about the Expedition.
Wilson gave his evidence in a half-hearted way.
The coroner asked Wilson what he was hiding.
Wilson replied that he had nothing to tell.
From that day Wilson and the narrator hardly exchanged ten words despite being together on the vessel.
Standing alone on a floe one day, the narrator hissed with clenched fist that he could kill Wilson if he dared suspect Clodagh of poisoning Peters.
They knew the ice was in awful upheaval around them.
As they fell asleep they heard distant booming and cracklings, possibly the tempest stirring the ocean beneath the ice.
They slept deeply, within ten miles of the Pole.
In his sleep the narrator felt as though someone shook his shoulder urging him up.
At midnight the narrator throws himself into his old berth.
The engines have fallen silent, and he hears the silence of their ghost as if haunted by them.
He sometimes startles from sleep, horrified by the sound of an exploding iceberg or a bumping floe.
Passing the fjord-mouth where Aadheim lay, the narrator suddenly turns the helm to port and makes for land.
Within half an hour he is moving up an opening in the land between mountains.
The arm of water curves so sharply that the scene changes every few minutes.
The vessel crawls slowly up, and he can see nothing behind him but a land-locked gleam like a lake.
The narrator crosses the yard and climbs a wooden spiral stair in twilight.
He picks his way among five or six vague forms fallen on the stair.
He tries the door on the first landing and finds it locked.
He goes up to the second landing, where the door is open.
He steps reluctantly inside into pitch darkness, the window-stores being drawn, and hesitates.
Under a Gothic arch the narrator sees a little house of rubble with rags beaten tightly into the window sashes to keep out the poison.
He goes in and finds the door of that room open, its edges also apparently stuffed.
An old man and woman lie dead on the threshold.
He conjectures that hunger or lack of oxygen drove them out and the still-active poison instantly killed them.
The narrator finds no newspapers dated later than soon after the 17th July, about three months after his arrival at the Pole.
The papers he found contained nothing scientific, only prayers and despairings.
On arriving in London he heads straight for the office of the Times.
He stops at a chemist's in Oxford Street for a bottle of antiseptic to hold near his nose.
At the square where the paper was printed he finds the ground closely strewn with clothing from many nations, muddled and mauled.
From around Whitby and the moors the narrator goes on to Darlington, near his home.
He refuses to continue toward home and lounges indecisively for two days.
He then sets out for Richmond and the lead mines around Arkengarth Dale near Reeth.
Some of the faces he sees there almost seem to speak to him in a broad dialect he knows.
In another dipple-region at a higher level the narrator nearly faints on reaching an area of after-damp where there had been an explosion.
The bodies there lie hairless, devastated and grotesque.
He retires from that area but does not stop searching every other quarter.
He does not go up by the pumping-shaft rope-ladder until nearly six.
Standing later at Cornwall Point, with a view of the crags at Land's End and no house in sight, he finishes what he calls his official search.
The narrator finds the shop door locked, as nearly all London shop-doors are.
He looks about near the ground and in a cart for something heavy.
He cuts a labourer's heavy boot from a shrivelled foot.
He beats at the glass with it until it shatters, knocks away the bottom splinters, and enters.
He feels no horror or sickness at the breaking glass, being calm and steady.
He recalls that eight months earlier he had left London a poor cowering wight, and now returns as the Sultan.
The narrator takes a phonograph with microphone diaphragm and a boxful of record-cylinders.
He puts them in the car, disliking the strong peach-odour in the closed shop.
He drives southward and westward through by-streets looking for a house to shelter in from the cold wind.
He sees the Parliament-house and goes there, turning river-ward by Westminster Hall to Palace Yard.
He carries his two parcels in along a line of purple-dusted busts.
He sets the boxes on a table beside what he takes to be the Mace, and sits down to listen.
One morning after four months the narrator wakes in his cell realizing he had burned Monpont overnight.
He is so overcome with regret that for two days he paces the nave, hardly eating, wondering if he is already mad.
The carved angels, wood-work, door and vault all seem to him conscious of him and his heart.
At about four on the second afternoon he falls down at an altar praying God to have mercy on his soul.
In the midst of praying he is up and away, gets into the motor, and does not return to Vauclaire for a month.
He leaves burned desolation behind him, including Bordeaux, Lebourne and Bergerac.
He returns to Vauclaire, feels a deep repentance, and humbles himself before his Maker.
Captain Tombarel's face whitens.
The narrator follows the direction of his gaze eastward.
He sees ten monstrous waterspouts about eight kilomètres away, reaching high up.
The spouts stand in one straight line at regular intervals of about nine hundred mètres.
They neither wander nor waver like waterspouts, being hewn pillars of uniform diameter.
He reckons them about fifty mètres in girth.
The narrator had thought the Voices were done with him and had not heard them for twenty years.
Today the Voices broke in upon his consciousness with brawling impassioned suddenness, and he heard them.
He blames his idleness, inaction and brooding for undermining his spirit.
Immediately after eating at noon that day he told himself he had been duped by the palace.
He says he wasted himself in building, hoping for peace, and there is no peace.

The narrator recalls seeing the turbaned Bashi-bazouk with his long sword, softas on the great wall of Stamboul, beggars, a street-merchant with a tray of food, a bear-shewer, a Barbary organ, and the night-watchman crying 'Fire!'
He remarks it is strange that the old life has come back to his fancy vividly for the first time, though he has been there several times lately.
He has gone out to the plains beyond the walls, where the city looks like nothing but minarets shooting through cypress-tops.
He seemed to see the wild muezzin at a summit crying the midday prayer.
The narrator lies still in the same pose without stirring, sick and dry-mouthed.
He resolves to wait and be artful as a snake, making no sound.
After some minutes he becomes conscious that his eyes are leering in one fixed direction.
The fact that he has a sense of direction proves to him that he really did hear something.
She takes the food but looks foolish and does not eat.
The narrator puts a little into her mouth with his forefinger, after which she hungrily eats it all.
He also gives her gingerbread, bonbons, Krishnu wine and anisette.
He sets out again, gruffly telling her to stay there, leaving her sitting on the well peering after him.
Before he reaches the ogival bazaar-portal he looks back and sees her limping after him.
The narrator cannot resist shouting a sudden 'Hi!'
She scrambles to her feet like a spring-bok.
He points at the drawing, smiling.
She mincingly presses her lips, shakes her head and coos a fond laugh.
He tells her she is a clever little wretch, and she cocks her eye trying to divine his meaning.
He goes on gruffly that she is clever as a serpent, saying that formerly the Black used the serpent but now it is the White.
The narrator tells her to go inside and reveals a secret: he picked musk-roses in the wood and wound them into a wreath for her head.
He says the wreath is on the pearl tripod in the second room to the left.
He tells her to put it on, bring the harp, and play to him.
She runs off with a little cry and returns, sitting crowned in the gold.
Three months and twenty-seven days after the earthquake, having covered only about 900 English miles, the narrator anchors in the Venice lagoon on the morning of 10th September.
He arrives in a Maltese speronare he had found and partially cleaned at Trieste.
He then passes up the Canalazzo in a gondola.
He tells Leda he will pitch his Patriarch tent in Venice.
He notes that he was driven still further westward.
She breaks the silence by asking whether she has not done wrong again.
The narrator hurriedly assures her she has not done wrong.
He says he could not suppose she would count up the days, and calls her considerate.
She asks 'Tell Leda?' and he suggests she might come fishing with him.
She softly exclaims 'O luck!'
The narrator is pierced by a sense of his own base cowardice and weakness but cannot help it.
The narrator and she drive into the dark town of Havre in a four-seat motor-car about ten in the evening of 29th December.
The night is raw and bleak and she is bitterly cramped with cold.
He drives to the quays and stops at the Maire's large palatial house overlooking the sea, where she sleeps while he occupies another nearby.
The next morning he is early astir and searches the mairie for a map of the town.
He also finds a Bottin there, which lets him locate the Telephone Exchange.
The bewildering character of the islands makes landing difficult.
The swirling flood carries the canoe in to shore and then sweeps it out again.
The willow branches tear their hands as they seize them to stop the canoe.
They pull many yards of sandy bank into the water before shooting into a backwater and beaching the bows in spray.
They lie panting and laughing on the hot yellow sand, sheltered from the wind in the blazing sun.
The feeling never quite leaves the narrator, even while pitching the tent in a hurricane of wind and building a fire.
The feeling bothers and perplexes him and robs the camping-ground of much of its charm.
The narrator says nothing about it to his companion, whom he considers devoid of imagination.
He reasons he could never have explained what he meant, and that his companion would have laughed stupidly at him.
The companion proposes dragging the canoe close to the tent so they can leave at a moment's notice.
He says he will sleep in his clothes.
He is off climbing along the bank, and the narrator hears his jolly laugh.
A moment later he calls out "By Jove!"
The narrator turns to look but cannot see him because the willows hide him.
The narrator watches the bushes moving together and shaking their heads.
He notices their leaves twirl even when there is no wind.
They seem to move of their own will, as if alive.
They touch his sense of the horrible.
They stand in the moonlight like an army surrounding the camp, ready to attack.
The narrator imagines the willows coming alive, rising up and sweeping down on them from the swamps before settling.
As he looks, it is easy to imagine them creeping nearer and huddling together in hostile masses.
He could have sworn their appearance changed and their ranks pressed closer together.
A night-bird gives a shrill melancholy cry overhead.
The piece of bank he is standing on is undermined by the flood and falls into the river with a splash, nearly making him lose his balance.
Half-way out of the tent on all fours, the narrator notices the tops of the bushes opposite making shapes against the sky.
He sits back on his haunches and stares.
He sees indeterminate shapes among the willows, opposite and slightly above him.
As the branches sway in the wind they seem to group around the shapes into monstrous outlines shifting under the moon.
He sees these things about fifty feet in front of him.
Something impels the narrator to creep farther out onto the sand and stand upright.
He feels the ground still warm under his bare feet and the wind tearing at his hair and face.
The roar of the river bursts upon his ears.
He concludes these sensations are real and that his senses are working normally.
The figures keep rising from earth to heaven in a great silent spiral.
The sight overwhelms him with a deep emotion of worship.
The narrator questions whether his reason is arguing uselessly from the small standard of what he knows.
He knows the great column of figures rose darkly into the sky for what seemed a long time and felt entirely real.
Then the figures suddenly vanish.
Once they are gone, fear comes down on him in a cold rush.
A bird utters its morning cry.
A string of duck passes overhead with whirring flight in the twilight.
The wind whirls dry stinging sand about the narrator's bare feet.
He walks round the tent and goes a little way into the bush so he can see across the river.
Seeing the endless sea of bushes stretching to the horizon in the dawn light, he is seized again by the same indefinable distress.
The narrator paces out on the sand the distances between the willows and the tent, noting the shortest one.
He crawls stealthily back into his blankets.
His companion appears to be still sleeping soundly, which the narrator is glad of.
He reasons that if his experiences are not corroborated he could find strength to deny them.
He thinks that in daylight he could persuade himself it was all a hallucination of the night.
The Swede eats very little breakfast and for once does not smoke his pipe.
He keeps the map spread open beside him and studies its markings.
The narrator says they had better get off sharp in an hour, hoping to draw a confession out of him.
The Swede answers "Rather! If they'll let us."
The narrator asks who will let them, suggesting the elements.
The Swede, keeping his eyes on the map, replies that he means the powers of the awful place, whoever they are.
The Swede turns away laughing a little and says the narrator can explain everything.
The narrator calls after him that the same wind caught the steering paddle and flung it near the bank, where it fell in with the next lump of crumbling bank.
The Swede shouts back "I see" and looks at the narrator before disappearing among the willow bushes.
Alone, the narrator's first thought is that one of them must have done it and it was not him.
His second thought is that it is impossible either of them did it.
The narrator remarks that the place must be lonely and that otters are shy things.
The Swede interrupts to ask whether the narrator really thinks it was an otter.
The narrator demands to know what else it could have been.
The Swede says he saw it first and at first it seemed much bigger than an otter.
The narrator replies that the sunset up-stream magnified it.
The Swede looks at him absently, his mind on other thoughts.
The narrator cries that the place is queer enough without imagining things.
He insists the boat was an ordinary boat and the man in it an ordinary man going downstream fast.
He insists the otter really was an otter.
The Swede looks steadily at him with the same grave expression and is not annoyed.
The narrator takes courage from the Swede's silence.
The sound seems to come to them out of the darkness from the waste of swamps and willows opposite.
It repeats at regular intervals.
The narrator judges it is neither a bell nor a distant steamer's hooting.
He likens it to an immense gong hung far up in the sky, struck over and over with a muffled metallic note.
His heart quickens as he listens.
The narrator suggests the sound is wind blowing in the sand-funnels or bushes rubbing together after the storm.
His friend answers that it comes off the whole swamp and from everywhere at once, ignoring the explanation.
The friend says it comes from the willow bushes somehow.
The narrator objects that the wind has dropped and the willows can hardly make a noise by themselves.
The friend answers that they hear it because the wind has dropped and it was drowned before.
The answer frightens the narrator, who knows intuitively it is true.
The Swede mutters that he hopes so, unless they are claimed first as victims for the sacrifice, and laughs foolishly.
He drags the sack into the tent for safety.
The narrator hears him mumbling indistinctly to himself and ignores the words.
They eat their meal almost in silence, avoiding each other's eyes and keeping the fire bright.
They wash up and prepare for the night.
Once they are smoking with nothing to do, the narrator's apprehension grows more acute.
The Swede says that to name them is to reveal, and their only hope is to ignore them so they may be ignored.
The narrator asks whether that applies even in thought.
The Swede, extremely agitated, says especially in thought, because their thoughts make spirals in that other world, and they must keep them out of their minds at all costs.
The narrator rakes the fire together to hold off the darkness.
He longs for the sun as never before in the blackness of that night.
The Swede suddenly asks whether the narrator was awake all last night.
The narrator asks the Swede what he makes of the hollows or sand-funnels in the ground around them.
The Swede cries "No!", forgetting to whisper in his excitement.
He says he dare not put the thought into words and is glad the narrator has not guessed it.
He says They have put the thought into his mind and urges the narrator to prevent them putting it into his.
He drops his voice back to a whisper, and the narrator does not press him to explain.
The narrator supposes it was a violent reaction after the strain of living among impossible things.
The spell lifts from his heart for about a minute, leaving him free and unafraid.
He looks up at his friend opposite.
He laughs in the Swede's face and calls him a damned old pagan, an imaginative idiot and a superstitious idolater.
He stops in the middle, seized again by the old horror.
He tries to smother the sound of his own voice as something sacrilegious.
The bushes fail to support the narrator's weight, and he and the Swede fall in a struggling heap on the sand.
The narrator hardly knows what is happening.
He is conscious of an enveloping icy fear that seems to pluck his nerves out and twist them.
His eyes are tightly shut and something chokes him in the throat.
He feels his consciousness expanding into space, then feels he is losing it altogether and about to die.
The narrator feels something besides the blanket pressing on him and first thinks his companion has rolled onto his mattress.
He calls to him and sits up.
It comes to him that the tent is surrounded.
The sound of multitudinous soft pattering is audible outside again.
He calls to his companion again, louder, and gets no answer.
He notices the snoring has stopped and that the tent flap is down.
The Swede says the river is falling at last and he is glad of it.
The narrator says the humming has stopped too.
The Swede looks up quietly with his normal expression, apparently remembering everything except his own suicide attempt.
He says everything has stopped "because—" and then hesitates.
The narrator, forcing a laugh, finishes it as "Because 'They've found another victim'?"
The Swede answers "Exactly!"

In the darkness Conan hears a sound ahead of him — bare feet shuffling or cloth swishing on stone.

He pushes against the door without result.
His sword-point finds no crack, the door fitting its frame as if molded there.

Kasatsky vows to serve his beloved Tsar with all his soul.
When Kasatsky takes up his commission, his mother and sister move to Moscow and then to the country estate.
Kasatsky gives half his property to his sister and keeps only enough to live in his expensive Guards regiment.
He appears to be an ordinary brilliant young Guards officer, but intense and complex strivings go on inside him.

Kasatsky proposes and is accepted.
He is surprised how easily he gained such happiness.
Blinded by love, he does not realize what almost the whole town knows: his fiancée had been the Emperor Nicholas's mistress the year before.
The next day he applies for furlough and for his discharge.
Pretending to be ill so as to see nobody, he goes away to the country.
He spends the summer at his village putting his affairs in order.
At summer's end he does not go back to Petersburg but enters a monastery and becomes a monk.
His mother writes trying to dissuade him, and he replies that he feels God's call above all other considerations.
Only his sister, as proud and ambitious as he, understands him.
The profession is an important event in his inner life.
He had previously felt great consolation and exaltation when taking communion.
Officiating himself, the preparation fills him with ecstatic, deep emotion.
That feeling later becomes more and more deadened.
Officiating once in a depressed mood, he feels the service's effect on him will not last.
The feeling does weaken until only habit remains.
